presentingComplaint: Two days of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia in an otherwise well young adult.
history: Previously healthy 24-year-old man with a 2-day history of frontal-occipital headache, low-to-moderate grade fever, marked photophobia and neck discomfort. Reports a preceding week of coryza and a self-limiting diarrhoeal illness in a flatmate. No confusion, no seizures, no focal weakness, no rash. No recent travel, no TB contact, immunocompetent, not on immunosuppression. Presentation is late summer (enteroviral season).
examination: Alert and fully oriented (GCS 15), looks uncomfortable but not toxic. Neck stiffness with positive Kernig sign; photophobia. No papilloedema on fundoscopy, no focal neurological deficit, no cranial nerve palsy. No petechial or purpuric rash. Kernig/Brudzinski positive but the patient remains lucid between examinations.
imaging: CT head prior to LP (young, no focal deficit, immunocompetent, alert) — normal, no mass lesion or midline shift; performed only to exclude contraindication where clinically indicated.
microbiology: CSF bacterial culture negative at 48h; CSF multiplex PCR positive for enterovirus. HSV-1/2 and VZV PCR negative. Blood cultures negative.
citations: IDSA Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis 2004 (differentiation of aseptic vs bacterial meningitis)
stewardship: Not applicable as a viral illness, but standard of care: because bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded at presentation, give empiric IV ceftriaxone (+ aciclovir if any encephalitic features) after blood cultures/LP, then STOP antibiotics once CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, negative Gram stain and negative bacterial culture/positive enteroviral PCR. Management is supportive (analgesia, fluids); most enteroviral cases are self-limiting.
contraindications: Ceftriaxone in documented severe beta-lactam anaphylaxis (use alternative)
Avoid LP before imaging if focal deficit, papilloedema, immunocompromise, seizures or reduced GCS
Aciclovir requires renal-adjusted dosing and adequate hydration
edgeCases: Partially treated bacterial meningitis can mimic aseptic meningitis with lymphocytic CSF — low CSF glucose or high protein argues against viral
HSV can cause aseptic meningitis (usually benign) but HSV encephalitis is a medical emergency — behavioural change, seizures or focal deficit should trigger empiric aciclovir
Drug-induced (NSAID, IVIG) and Mollaret recurrent lymphocytic meningitis are non-infective mimics
expectedMaiK: Classic enteroviral aseptic meningitis in an immunocompetent young adult: lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose and negative Gram stain supports a viral cause. Cover empirically for bacterial meningitis until CSF confirms a viral picture, then de-escalate; treatment is supportive with an excellent prognosis.
expectedNextQuestions: Any altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurological signs to suggest encephalitis?
Any immunosuppression, recent neurosurgery, or antibiotics taken before presentation (partially-treated bacterial)?
expectedInvestigations: Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count/differential, protein, glucose (with paired serum glucose), Gram stain and culture
CSF viral multiplex PCR (enterovirus, HSV-1/2, VZV)
regressionAssertions: differential must include MENINGITIS (bacterial) given inability to exclude it at presentation
must not recommend continuing antibiotics once CSF confirms lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and negative Gram stain/culture
